name: The Aesthetic Attitude
statement: A special disinterested way of attending to things, contemplating them for their own sake.
meaning: The aesthetic attitude is a distinctive way of attending to or perceiving an object, a work of art or a natural scene, that on some theories constitutes aesthetic experience and makes appreciation aesthetic. Aesthetic-attitude theories hold that what makes an experience aesthetic is not the object but the special mode of attention the perceiver brings to it. The hallmark of that mode is disinterestedness: attending to the object for its own sake, without practical, personal, or instrumental interest, not out of desire, use, or self-interest. The idea of disinterestedness emerged in eighteenth-century British aesthetics, in Shaftesbury and Hutcheson, and is central to Kant's account of the judgment of taste as a disinterested pleasure, in his Critique of the Power of Judgment of 1790. Schopenhauer described a will-less contemplation that frees us momentarily from the striving of the will. In the twentieth century, Edward Bullough, in his 1912 essay on psychical distance, held that aesthetic appreciation requires putting the object out of gear with our practical needs, a certain psychical distance, and that both too little distance, under-distancing, and too much, over-distancing, spoil the experience. Jerome Stolnitz, in 1960, defined the aesthetic attitude as disinterested and sympathetic attention to and contemplation of any object of awareness whatever, for its own sake alone. The tradition was sharply attacked by George Dickie, whose 1964 essay The Myth of the Aesthetic Attitude denied there is any special mode of attention.
mechanism: Aesthetic-attitude theories explain the aesthetic by pointing to how a perceiver attends rather than to what is attended. On this approach, the same object, a landscape, a building, a piece of music, can be regarded in an ordinary, practical, interested way, as something to use, own, or exploit, or in a special aesthetic way, contemplated for its own sake with no ulterior interest; it is adopting the latter mode of attention that makes the experience aesthetic. The defining feature is disinterestedness, a suspension of practical concern and desire, so that one dwells on the object itself, its qualities and appearance, rather than on what it can do for oneself. Different theorists specify the attitude differently. Kant located it in a pleasure that is disinterested, indifferent to the object's usefulness or even its existence, and merely contemplative. Schopenhauer intensified this into a will-less contemplation that lifts the subject out of the ceaseless striving of the will. Bullough recast the attitude as psychical distance: to appreciate aesthetically one must put the object out of gear with one's actual practical self, viewing it at a psychical remove, and he noted that the distance can be lost in two opposite ways, by too little distance, being so practically or emotionally engaged that one cannot appreciate, and by too much, being so detached that nothing engages one. Stolnitz distilled the tradition into disinterested and sympathetic attention to any object for its own sake alone. Against this whole family of views, Dickie argued that there is no distinctive disinterested state at all, only attention that is more or less close and variously directed.

examples.text: The aesthetic attitude attends to an object for its own sake, without practical, personal, or instrumental interest.
Bullough held aesthetic appreciation requires putting the object out of gear with practical need, at a psychical distance.
Dickie argued there is no special disinterested attention, only attending versus not attending, calling the attitude a myth.

variants.name: Psychical distance
variants.text: Bullough's version, requiring a distance from practical concern, spoiled by both under-distancing and over-distancing.

variants.name: Disinterested attention
variants.text: Stolnitz's account of the aesthetic attitude as disinterested and sympathetic contemplation for its own sake alone.

whyItMatters: The aesthetic attitude is a major tradition in modern aesthetics, offering a distinctive answer to the foundational question of what makes an experience, or an object, aesthetic. Rather than seeking a special class of aesthetic objects or properties, attitude theories locate the aesthetic in the perceiver's mode of attention, in a disinterested contemplation of things for their own sake, and this move carried the influential eighteenth-century notion of disinterestedness, from Shaftesbury and Hutcheson through Kant, into twentieth-century theory. It gives an appealing account of how almost anything, a work of art, a natural scene, even an ordinary object, can become the focus of aesthetic appreciation when regarded in the right spirit, and Bullough's notion of psychical distance and Stolnitz's disinterested attention became standard reference points. The tradition also provoked one of the most consequential debates in analytic aesthetics: George Dickie's argument that the aesthetic attitude is a myth, that there is no distinctive disinterested state but only ordinary attention differently directed, pushed the field away from attitude theories and toward institutional and other accounts. Whether embraced or rejected, the aesthetic attitude frames enduring questions about the nature of the aesthetic. As the idea that a special mode of attention makes experience aesthetic, it is a central position in the philosophy of art.

working.text: attend to the object for its own sake, suspending desire, use, and self-interest.
put the object out of gear with practical need, at a psychical distance, neither too near nor too far.
dwell on the object's qualities and appearance in disinterested, sympathetic attention.

limits: The aesthetic attitude faces a powerful skeptical challenge and internal difficulties. George Dickie, in The Myth of the Aesthetic Attitude of 1964, argued that there is no special mode of disinterested attention: the supposed contrast between disinterested and interested attention collapses into the ordinary contrast between attending and not attending, since a spy and an aesthete watching the same play both simply attend to it, so disinterested attention is a myth and cannot ground the aesthetic. This influential attack pushed aesthetics away from attitude theories. There are also difficulties in specifying the attitude precisely: disinterestedness is hard to define without circularity, and Bullough's psychical distance, with its twin failures of under- and over-distancing, is more a suggestive metaphor than a rigorous criterion. It is disputed whether any purely subjective mode of attention could make an experience aesthetic without reference to the object's features. Some attributions and datings reward care: Bullough's essay dates to 1912, Stolnitz's book to 1960, Dickie's essay to 1964, and figures such as Schopenhauer are cited with volumes of differing dates. So the aesthetic attitude robustly locates the aesthetic in disinterested attention, understood as an influential tradition sharply challenged by Dickie's argument that no such distinctive attitude exists.
misreadings: The aesthetic attitude's disinterestedness is not indifference or lack of engagement; it is attention freed from practical and self-interested concern, a sympathetic contemplation for the object's own sake. It is not a claim that aesthetic value lies in the object alone, since attitude theories locate the aesthetic in the perceiver's mode of attention. And it is not an uncontested notion, since Dickie argued there is no such special attitude at all, so treating disinterestedness as detachment, the aesthetic as purely in the object, or the attitude as beyond doubt, misreads the tradition.
origin: The tradition in modern aesthetics, rooted in eighteenth-century disinterestedness and developed by Bullough's psychical distance and Stolnitz, that a special disinterested mode of attention makes experience aesthetic, challenged by Dickie's 1964 myth argument.
